name: Nori Robotics

team.summary: Founded by Antonio, who previously did robotics research at Columbia and worked on human demonstrations before building Nori Robotics in San Francisco.

evidence.quote: I started working on Nori while doing robotics research at Columbia.
We assemble each robot in San Francisco and have designed it to be easy to manufacture and repair

product.summary: Nori A3 is a $1,688 bimanual mobile robot featuring 19 degrees of freedom, a telescoping lift, differential wheeled base, and multiple cameras, designed for robotics developers and researchers.

evidence.quote: We build a $1,688 bimanual mobile robot in San Francisco for robotics developers and researchers.

size_hint.summary: Targeting robotics developers, researchers, and hobbyists looking for affordable bimanual hardware.

competitors.summary: Mention of K-scale labs and low-cost Chinese robots as comparative platforms.

evidence.quote: Curious what the business model of this is to make the company sustainable. Asking that because I was part of the K-scale labs community and sad to see it shut down due to the competition with low-cost chinese robots
evidence.author: TristanX

why_now.summary: Advances in low-cost hardware components and open-source SDKs enabling sub-$2,000 humanoid and bimanual robotics development.

evidence.quote: Getting this under $2,000 was the main engineering challenge.

risks.risk: Hardware reliability and limitations of RC-style servos leading to jerky or imprecise motions.

evidence.quote: The biggest problem is they are using RC style servos. This is why all the arm motions are jerky and lack precision.

risks.risk: Skepticism over marketing claims regarding autonomous household task capabilities like cooking and folding clothes.

evidence.quote: So I guess my main question is: What do you hope to accomplish by shamelessly lying? I mean, beyond the lack of shame, you're selling a product here, so are you not at least afraid of the lawsuits?

founder_depth.why: Founder has a relevant academic robotics research background at Columbia and has iterated on hardware designs, but limited prior commercial shipping history is detailed.

evidence.quote: I started working on Nori while doing robotics research at Columbia.

shipping_evidence.why: Product is live with orders, a simulator, and an open SDK repository available, but engineering depth on public code repositories is minimal.

evidence.quote: We’ve shipped our first robot and are building the next batch.
Our open SDK includes teleoperation and demonstration tools: https://github.com/Nori-Robotics/nori-sdk-py

demand_signal.why: High Hacker News engagement with over 200 points and 66 comments showing strong initial interest from developers and hobbyists.

defensibility.why: Low-cost hardware built from off-the-shelf components with open source SDKs and 3D files makes it susceptible to commoditization and easy to copy.

evidence.quote: We also built a browser-based simulator so you can try it out: https://lab.norirobotics.com/nori/model
we offer 3D files to print repairs

analysis.thesis_fit_reason: Nori Robotics builds physical humanoid robot hardware and devices, which are explicitly out of scope for the software and infrastructure thesis.
analysis.case_summary: Strong initial developer engagement and low price point for bimanual robotics, offset by the physical product category being out of scope and concerns over hardware limitations.
would_change_my_mind: Expansion into pure AI-native control software for third-party hardware
Transition of the business model to focus primarily on agentic software infrastructure
Demonstration of sustained commercial scale in developer software tools
data_gaps: Detailed financial metrics and recurring software revenue breakdown
Comprehensive telemetry and safety compliance documentation
Complete bill of materials and supplier agreements
